normai.name: NormAI
normai.problem: LLM pipelines generate huge legal reports where the same concept appears written in dozens of different ways, so nothing is ready for analysis.
normai.approach: Each project is configured once, with a column dictionary, cleaning rules and AI-assisted classification. Every upload then runs through an async pipeline.
normai.outcome: Analysts upload, come back later and download a clean file. Task time down 99.8%, and 1st place in Innovation at the IDP × JusBrasil sprint.

u.label: Analyst
u.why: Uploads raw spreadsheets and comes back later. Nothing blocks the browser.

fe.label: Next.js
fe.why: Login, projects, dictionary, status and dashboard in one typed app.

api.label: FastAPI
api.why: Async API that queues each upload as a job and reports progress.

db.label: PostgreSQL
db.why: Projects keep their dictionary and cleaning rules, so setup happens once.

ai.label: AI step
ai.why: Classifies the values rules cannot map, so one concept ends up written one way.

oficina.name: Oficina ES
oficina.problem: A team needed answers grounded in its own documents, behind real authentication, without building a backend from scratch.
oficina.approach: n8n workflows handle login, token refresh and an auth guard. Drive documents are chunked and embedded, and an agent answers with vector search and chat memory.
oficina.outcome: A protected Q&A endpoint over the team’s documents, running on open models, deployed with Docker and Caddy.

u.label: User
u.why: Asks questions in plain language, only after logging in.

n8n.label: n8n
n8n.why: Auth, ingestion and the agent are workflows, not a custom backend.

vec.label: pgvector
vec.why: Documents are chunked and embedded, so answers come from the team’s own files.

llm.label: Ollama
llm.why: Open models running locally. Documents never leave the server.

auth.label: Supabase
auth.why: Real authentication and sessions in front of the Q&A endpoint.

fluxo.name: NexAI Fluxogram
fluxo.problem: Executives needed to understand how NexAI turns strategy into product across 14 business verticals, without reading a process manual.
fluxo.approach: An interactive flowchart: Strategy → Requirements → Design Thinking → Development, with each vertical as its own explorable path.
fluxo.outcome: Used to present the product process to non-technical stakeholders in one screen.

a.label: Strategy
a.why: Every initiative starts from a business goal.

b.label: Requirements
b.why: Goals become product requirements before any screen exists.

c.label: Design Thinking
c.why: Ideas are prototyped and tested with people before code.

v.label: 14 verticals
v.why: Each vertical follows the same path, with its own branch.

sharebite.name: ShareBite
sharebite.line: Food donation platform built in a weekend.
sharebite.problem: Food that could be donated gets thrown away, partly because donors are not sure it meets ANVISA rules.
sharebite.approach: A Streamlit interface, a Flask API and MongoDB, with an AI agent that checks each donation against ANVISA criteria and interactive impact reports.
sharebite.outcome: Built in 20 hours. 1st place at the 5th IDP Hackathon.

u.label: Streamlit
u.why: Donors and receivers use one simple interface.

api.label: Flask
api.why: A small API keeps donations, requests and matches in one place.

db.label: MongoDB
db.why: Flexible documents for donations that vary a lot in shape.

rep.label: Reports
rep.why: Interactive reports show how much food was saved.

ai.label: AI check
ai.why: An agent checks each donation against ANVISA criteria before it is listed.

orbitas.name: Órbitas
orbitas.problem: How close can a short Fourier series get to a real planetary orbit?
orbitas.approach: A simulation for every planet from Mercury to Neptune, comparing the approximation with the reference orbit, with tests and notebooks.
orbitas.outcome: An interactive CLI: pick a planet and watch the approximation converge.

a.label: Planet data
a.why: Reference orbits for every planet, Mercury to Neptune.

b.label: Fourier series
b.why: Each orbit approximated by a short sum of sines and cosines.

c.label: NumPy
c.why: Compares the approximation with the reference, term by term.

d.label: Matplotlib
d.why: Shows the error shrinking as terms are added.

e.label: CLI
e.why: Choose a planet and see it converge.

veritas.name: Veritas
veritas.line: Follow public projects from your phone.
veritas.problem: Public project data is scattered across official sources and hard to follow from a phone.
veritas.approach: A cross-platform app with its own backend that groups projects and sends alerts when something changes.
veritas.outcome: iOS and Android app from one TypeScript codebase, with setup guide and security policy in the repository.

a.label: React Native
a.why: One TypeScript codebase for iOS and Android.

b.label: Backend
b.why: Collects and groups public project data for the app.

c.label: Public data
c.why: Official sources, normalized so projects can be followed over time.

d.label: Alerts
d.why: Notifications when a followed project changes.

contratus.name: Contratus AI
contratus.problem: Reading a long contract to answer one question takes too long.
contratus.approach: RAG over contracts: documents are split into chunks, indexed as vectors and retrieved to ground every answer.
contratus.outcome: Upload a contract and ask questions in a chat, with answers grounded in the right clauses.

a.label: SvelteKit
a.why: Upload a contract and ask questions in a chat.

b.label: FastAPI
b.why: Chunks contracts and handles retrieval and answers.

c.label: Pinecone
c.why: Vector index, so answers come from the right clauses.

d.label: LLM
d.why: Answers only from the retrieved passages.

airq.name: Air Quality Pipeline
airq.problem: Air quality readings arrive continuously and need to be processed without losing events.
airq.approach: An event-driven pipeline: Kafka streams readings, Celery workers process them over Redis and RabbitMQ, results go to MinIO and a dashboard.
airq.outcome: Each stage scales on its own, and a Streamlit dashboard shows the processed data.

a.label: Sources
a.why: Air quality readings arrive as events.

b.label: Kafka
b.why: Decouples producers from processing, so nothing is lost.

c.label: Celery
c.why: Workers process and aggregate readings, with Redis and RabbitMQ underneath.

d.label: MinIO
d.why: Processed data stored as objects, S3-compatible.

e.label: Streamlit
e.why: Dashboard over the processed data, served with Flask.

stsw.name: Security & Testing
stsw.line: Black-box, white-box and BDD suites in Java, plus OWASP labs.
stsw.problem: One semester to cover black-box, white-box and behaviour-driven testing, then web security, with every assignment delivered as working code.
stsw.approach: A small classifier tested three ways: Gherkin scenarios bound to Cucumber steps, JUnit suites for five coverage criteria measured with JaCoCo, and a TestNG suite with HTML reports. Security work ran as OWASP Top 10 labs on deliberately vulnerable training apps.
stsw.outcome: 5 BDD scenarios, 38 white-box tests and 22 TestNG tests, plus 10 security labs documented with evidence. TestNG was also presented to the class as a workshop.

a.label: STSW course
a.why: Security & Software Testing at IDP. Each assignment is its own Maven project in a shared course repository.

b.label: Cucumber
b.why: Behaviour written first in plain language, then bound to step code.

c.label: White-box
c.why: Statement, decision, condition, condition/decision and path coverage over the same logic, checked with JaCoCo.

d.label: TestNG
d.why: Grouped suites with HTML reports, researched and presented to the class as a workshop.

e.label: Security labs
e.why: 10 challenges on deliberately vulnerable training apps, each solved and documented with evidence.

ekoparty.name: Ekoparty CTF
ekoparty.line: 4th place in a five-hour CTF, as the team's Web3 specialist.
ekoparty.problem: Ekoparty 2026's CTF: five hours, 32 challenges across seven categories, from malware and network traffic to smart contracts. We played as a team of two.
ekoparty.approach: I took Web3 while my teammate took reverse engineering. Weeks before, I built a searchable library of 75 problem-to-method patterns across 12 categories, wired into an AI-assisted triage workflow, so time on the clock went to solving, not searching.
ekoparty.outcome: Team nop finished 4th. My part: 3320 points, 11 solves and 2 first bloods, with every Web3 challenge solved. The writeups are public in English, Spanish and Portuguese, with live credentials redacted.

a.label: Arsenal
a.why: Built weeks ahead: each entry says how to recognise a kind of challenge and what has worked on it, searchable in seconds.

b.label: Ekoparty
b.why: Ekoparty 2026 CTF, October 9, 10:00 to 15:00, seven categories on one board.

c.label: Web3
c.why: Smart-contract challenges: read the code and find what it allows that it shouldn't. All five solved.

d.label: Scoreboard
d.why: A team of two in 4th place. My part: 3320 points, 11 solves and 2 first bloods.

e.label: Writeups
e.why: Every solve written up on one template, in three languages, with live credentials redacted.

kernel.name: OS Internals
kernel.line: A bootloader, a patched kernel, a new syscall and x86 assembly.
kernel.problem: Operating systems are usually learned from diagrams. This course asked for the real pieces, built and booted one by one.
kernel.approach: A 512-byte real-mode bootloader that loads a kernel and jumps to it; Linux 6.6 patched, compiled and booted in QEMU on a BusyBox initramfs; a new system call that works with a character driver; and weekly x86 assembly exercises.
kernel.outcome: Every piece boots in QEMU from a script or a Makefile, with per-step logs, plus 81 assembly files across 20 exercise sets.

a.label: x86 Assembly
a.why: Weekly exercises on registers, the stack and interrupts. The base for everything to the right.

b.label: Bootloader
b.why: One boot sector that loads a kernel from disk, passes a value in a register and jumps to it.

c.label: Linux 6.6
c.why: Kernel compiled from source with a patch applied, booted in QEMU.

d.label: Syscall
d.why: A new system call that prints from kernel space and works with a character driver.

e.label: initramfs
e.why: Minimal userspace: a static C program calls into the kernel and the answer shows up in dmesg.

sqlmap.name: SQLMap Seminar
sqlmap.line: Automated SQL injection assessment, demoed end to end in a lab.
sqlmap.problem: Show a class how automated vulnerability assessment works, live, without touching any system we weren't allowed to test.
sqlmap.approach: A deliberately vulnerable app runs in Docker as the only target. A Makefile drives every step, alone or chained, and a small Flask + Next.js console runs the same steps in front of the class. The assessment repeats across four difficulty levels.
sqlmap.outcome: A reproducible demo in one command, with docs, a timed script and slides. The hardest level uses prepared statements and holds, which closes the talk on the fix.

a.label: Console
a.why: One button per step and the tool's output live, so the class follows without reading a terminal.

b.label: Flask
b.why: Thin wrapper that runs the same Make targets the terminal uses.

c.label: Makefile
c.why: Every step runs alone or chained in one command, so the demo is reproducible.

d.label: SQLMap
d.why: Open-source scanner that finds and confirms the injection on its own.

e.label: DVWA
e.why: Deliberately vulnerable app in a container, the only target. Its hardest level uses prepared statements and holds.

tedax.name: Tedax
tedax.line: Terminal bomb-defusal game in C where every role is a thread.
tedax.problem: A concurrent programming project: a bomb squad where modules, defusers and benches compete for time, with no races or deadlocks.
tedax.approach: Each role runs in its own pthread: a generator posts modules, defuser threads take benches, a coordinator parses commands and a display thread redraws the ncurses UI. One mutex guards the game state, and condition variables wake threads on new modules, free benches and screen updates.
tedax.outcome: A playable terminal game with three difficulty levels, a queue per defuser and optional music through SDL2_mixer, built with a classmate.

a.label: Player
a.why: Types short commands that pick a defuser, a bench and a module, or leaves them out for defaults.

b.label: Coordinator
b.why: Parses each command, fills in the defaults and hands out the work.

c.label: Defusers
c.why: Each defuser holds a bench while it works, with at most one job queued.

d.label: Game state
d.why: One mutex guards the state. Condition variables wake threads instead of polling.

e.label: ncurses UI
e.why: Redraws when signalled, so the screen never shows a half-updated state.

ba.label: NormAI before and after
ba.title: Same product. My design.
ba.body: Rebuilt in my own tone: calmer, clearer, nicer to use. Drag to compare.
ba.headline: Upload. Come back. Done.
ba.notesBefore: Dense screens, every option visible at once, little hierarchy. It worked, but it was tiring to use.
ba.notesAfter: Same features, fewer decisions per screen: clear steps, generous spacing and one obvious next action.
